learn.intro: A break-in at the Democratic Party's offices in 1972 grew into a scandal that forced President Nixon to resign in 1974 — the only US President ever to do so — and led to new laws limiting presidential power.

sections.title: 1. Reasons for and key features of the scandal

blocks.p: Nixon was secretive and suspicious of opponents; he kept an 'enemies list' and his Committee for the Re-election of the President (nicknamed CREEP) used dirty tricks. On 17 June 1972 five men were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee's offices in the Watergate building in Washington, DC. They were linked to CREEP.

Nixon won a landslide re-election in November 1972, but Washington Post journalists Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, helped by a secret source ('Deep Throat'), kept investigating. A Senate committee held televised hearings in 1973. White House counsel John Dean testified that Nixon was involved in a cover-up, and an aide revealed that Nixon secretly taped conversations in his office.

Nixon refused to hand over the tapes. In October 1973 he had the special prosecutor, Archibald Cox, sacked (the 'Saturday Night Massacre'). In July 1974 the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in US v Nixon that he must release them, and the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment. One tape — the 'smoking gun' — showed he had ordered the cover-up. Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974.

sections.title: 2. Impact on Nixon, US politics and new laws

blocks.p: Nixon became the first President to resign. Gerald Ford became President. On 8 September 1974 Ford gave Nixon a full pardon for any crimes — many Americans were angry, and it probably helped Ford lose the 1976 election.
Trust in government fell sharply. Democrats made big gains in the 1974 congressional elections. The media's investigative role grew.

ul: War Powers Act (1973): limited the President's power to send troops into action without Congress's approval.
Election Campaign Act (1974): limits on campaign donations and spending; a Federal Election Commission.
Privacy Act (1974): limited how the government could collect and use information about individuals.
Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act (1974): stopped the President refusing to spend money Congress had approved.

evidence: 1974: Election Campaign Act; Privacy Act; Budget Control Act.

flashcards.q: Why did the Watergate scandal happen?
flashcards.a: Nixon's secrecy and suspicion of opponents; CREEP's dirty tricks; the attempted cover-up.
Woodward and Bernstein's reporting; the Senate hearings; John Dean's evidence; the secret tapes; US v Nixon.

flashcards.q: What was the Saturday Night Massacre?
flashcards.a: October 1973: Nixon had special prosecutor Archibald Cox sacked.

flashcards.q: Give two effects of Watergate on US politics.
flashcards.a: Nixon resigned; trust in government fell; Democrats gained in 1974; new laws limited presidential power.
Nixon was never tried; many saw it as a deal; it damaged Ford.
